builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
summary: This is a diagnostic finding, not a deployable method: it replaces nothing, but shows that treating SHAP/LIME attributions as statements about the underlying continuous quantity must give way to treating them as statements about the quantized effective input. Adoption costs a sensitivity audit—re-running explanations across candidate discretizations and comparing against a seed-noise floor—which adds compute and pipeline complexity for a constrained team. It can fail because the frozen-model design cannot separate representation effects from effective-input effects, and results derive from one dataset (UCI Adult), one model class (random forest), and one feature (age), so findings may not transfer.
rationale: For a production team shipping explanations, the actionable lesson is to prefer KernelSHAP over LIME for stability and to audit attributions against discretization before trusting them, but the paper validates this on a single tabular benchmark, so workload-specific testing is required rather than blanket adoption.

claims.statement: This is a diagnostic finding, not a deployable method: it replaces nothing, but shows that treating SHAP/LIME attributions as statements about the underlying continuous quantity must give way to treating them as statements about the quantized effective input. Adoption costs a sensitivity audit—re-running explanations across candidate discretizations and comparing against a seed-noise floor—which adds compute and pipeline complexity for a constrained team. It can fail because the frozen-model design cannot separate representation effects from effective-input effects, and results derive from one dataset (UCI Adult), one model class (random forest), and one feature (age), so findings may not transfer.

LIME is 2.5–4.6x less consistent across repeats than KernelSHAP under discretization of a continuous feature; SHAP's normalized attribution change exceeds LIME's in all conditions (rank-biserial 0.81–1.00), and 45–94% of instances show large SHAP attribution changes with no class flip.
